```{r}
#| label: setup-libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(fpp3)
library(knitr)
library(seasonal)
```

## 1. Time and Tsibbles

#retail_ts - Sourced manually from the U.S Census Bureau's Monthly Retail Trade Survey via FRED. It tracks monthly retail trade and food services sales in millions of dollars. It contains two series stacked in long format (RSAFS) which are seasonally adjusted and (RSAFSNA) which are not seasonally adjusted. Its index is Month and its key is series_id

#can_gas - Sourced form the fpp3 package, tracking monthly natural gas production in Canada measured in billions of cubic meters from Jan 1960 to Feb 2005. Its index is Month and it has no key since it contains a single univariate series.

```{r}
#| label: load-and-prep-data
# Read raw FRED retail sales CSV
retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/fredgraph.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)

# Reshape to long format
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>  
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>  
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), 
    names_to = "series_id", 
    values_to = "sales"
  )

# Build retail_ts tsibble
retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>  
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>  
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

# Create working copy of Canadian gas
can_gas <- canadian_gas |>  
  select(Month, Volume)

```

## Gap Checks

```{r}
#| label: check-gaps
has_gaps(retail_ts) |> kable(caption = "Gap Check: Retail Sales tsibble")
has_gaps(can_gas) |> kable(caption = "Gap Check: Canadian Gas tsibble")
```

## Monthly Production Averages

```{r}
#| label: can-gas-recent-summary
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>  
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan")) |> 
  mutate(
    year    = year(Month),         
    month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),         
    quarter = quarter(Month)
  )

can_gas_recent |>  
  as_tibble() |>  
  group_by(month) |>  
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume)) |> 
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Average Canadian Gas Production by Month (1990–Present)")
```

Highest Production month - Dec exhibits the highest average production volume due to winter heating demand.

Lowest Production Month - Jun exhibits the lowest average production volume.

## Quarterly Aggregation

```{r}
#| label: quarterly-gas
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>  
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>  
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>  
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Quarterly Canadian Natural Gas Production", x = "Quarter", y = "Volume") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Sum vs Mean - I used sum() rather than mean() because natural gas production is a flow variable representing cumulative volume produced over a time window, taking the average would yield average monthly production within a quarter rather than total quarterly output.

Seasonality - The quarterly series remains distinctly seasonal,exhibiting a clear repeating pattern across quarters.

## Visualizing Retail Sales and Gas Production

```{r}
#| label: autoplot-retail
retail_ts |>  
  autoplot(sales) +  
  labs(    
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",    
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",    
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL  
  ) +  
  theme_minimal()
```

Seasonal Adjustment Analysis - The not seasonally adjusted (NSA) series exhibits an recurring inter year pattern, featuring a sharp surge Dec followed by an immediate drop in Jan. The seasonally adjusted (SA) series smooths out this calendar driven noise while keeping the long run macroeconomic trend and major recessionary contractions completely intact.

```{r}
#| label: gas-custom-layer
can_gas |>  
  autoplot(Volume) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Monthly Natural Gas Production with LOESS Smooth",
    subtitle = "Featuring a smooth trend curve over raw monthly volume",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Volume (Billion m³)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Layer explanation - I added a geom_smooth() layer to visibly highlight the overall secular trend in gas production independent of seasonal oscillations.

## 2. Transformations

## Log Transformations

```{r}
#| label: log-transformations
can_gas <- can_gas |> mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(log_volume) + 
  labs(title = "Log of Canadian Monthly Natural Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Canadian gas log evaluation - Seasonal swings in raw gas production grow larger as overall volume increases through the 1970s and 1980s. Taking logarithms stabilizes the variance pf these seasonal oscillations, making constant percentage shifts appear as constant absolute movements, which benefits linear models.

```{r}
#| label: retail-log
retail_nsa_logged <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

retail_nsa_logged |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "Log of U.S. Retail Sales (NSA)", y = "log(Sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Retail sales log evaluation - The case for logging the NSA retail sales series is even stronger than for Canadian gas because retail sales display huge, multiplicative Dec holiday spikes that grow exponentially larger in absolute dollar terms over time.

## Growth Rates & Approximation

```{r}
#| label: growth-rates
can_gas <- can_gas |>  
  mutate(    
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),    
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume),
    growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff)
  )

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(growth_direct) + 
  labs(title = "Month-over-Month Direct Percentage Growth Rate", y = "Growth Rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(growth_gap) + 
  labs(title = "Absolute Approximation Gap (Direct vs. Log-Difference)", y = "Gap (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Approximation accuracy - The log difference approximation is extremely accurate in this context, with the absolute difference growth_gap remaining close to zero across almost all observations.

## SA vs NSA Growth Rates

```{r}
#| label: sa-vs-nsa-growth
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>  
  group_by_key() |>  
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>  
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>  
  autoplot(growth_mom) +  
  labs(    
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",    
    x = NULL, y = "Growth Rate (%)", color = NULL  
  ) +  
  theme_minimal()
```

Growth Rate Comparison - The month over month growth rate of the NSA series is significantly noisier than that of the SA series, exhibiting massive, recurring spikes and drops every year. This extreme volatility is driven by predictable calendar events and holiday shopping cycles, such as massive Dec retail surges followed by sharp Jan contractions. In contrast, seasonal adjustment filters out this predictable intr year calendar noise, leaving the SA growth rate much smoother and better reflective of true underlying economic momentum.

## 3. Seasonality 

## Season Plots

```{r}
#| label: season-plots
retail_ts |>  
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>  
  gg_season(sales) +  
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +  
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>  
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>  
  gg_season(sales) +  
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +  
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>  
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Logged Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Seasonal Plot observations -

Contrasting NSA and SA plots demonstrates that seasonal adjustment removes predictable annual peaks, flattening lines so they tightly on top of each other.

Canadian natural gas shows clear winter peaks driven by commercial and residential space heating demand, and late summer troughs.

## Subseries Plot

```{r}
#| label: subseries-plot
can_gas |>  
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +  
  labs(title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

##  X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment

```{r}
#| label: x13-decomposition
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>  
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>  
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>  
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

X-13 Component Analysis -
The seasonal factor peaks in December at roughly 15% to 20% above the underlying trend line. The amplitude of these seasonal factors varies moderately across decades.

```{r}
#| label: x13-comparison
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>  
  as_tibble() |>  
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>  
  left_join(    
    retail_ts |>      
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>      
      as_tibble() |>      
      transmute(Month, census = sales),    
    by = "Month"  ) |>  
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>  
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +  
  geom_line() +  
  labs(    
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",    
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"  
  ) +  
  theme_minimal()
```

Official vs Custom adjustment -

The custom default X-13 seasonal adjustment tracks the official Census Bureau series closely, staying within a fraction of a percent for most of the timeline. Deviations peak during economic shocks and major recessionary periods, where official procedures incorporate specialized outlier treatments and disaggregated component adjustments.

## Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Model

```{r}
#| label: tslm-model
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>  
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

can_gas_fit |>  
  tidy() |>  
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>  
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "TSLM Model Coefficients (Canadian Gas Log Volume)")
```

Estimated Average Monthly Growth Rate - The estimated coefficient on trend multiplied by 100 yields the average monthly percentage growth rate of 0.4% per month.

Most significant seasonal effect - The month of Jul/Aug exhibits the largest absolute t-statistic relative to the omitted base month.

```{r}
#| label: tslm-fit-plot
can_gas_fit |>  
  augment() |>  
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +  
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +  
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +  
  labs(
    title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",       
    y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL
  ) +  
  theme_minimal()
```

Fitted Line Evaluation -

The linear trend plus seasonal dummies model captures the broad upward trajectory and static annual seasonality well, but visibly fails when the true trend bends or when seasonal amplitudes shift over time.

## Residual Diagnostics & Ljung-Box Test

```{r}
#| label: tslm-residuals
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>  
  augment() |>  
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |> 
  kable(caption = "Ljung-Box Test Results (lag = 24)")
```

Residual analysis - The residuals do not resemble white noise. The ACF plot displays large, significant auto correlations across multiple lags, and the residual time series exhibits clear persistent patterns. The Ljung-Box test yields a p-value near 0, formally rejecting the null hypothesis of white noise.

## 4. Forecast Evaluation

## Expanding-Window Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| label: cv-expanding
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>  
  select(Month, Volume) |>  
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>  
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),        
    tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())
  ) |>  
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>  
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |> 
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Expanding-Window Forecast Accuracy (1-Step Ahead)")
```

Evaluation dates -

The evaluated forecasts range from January 1980 (month 241) to January 2005.

Accuracy Verdict -

The TSLM model achieves lower MAE and RMSE than SNAIVE, indicating superior overall forecast precision. Both error metrics agree on this ranking.

## Diebold–Mariano Test

```{r}
#| label: dm-test
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>  
  as_tibble() |>  
  left_join(
    as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),            
    by = "Month"
  ) |>  
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>  
  select(Month, .model, e) |>  
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>  
  na.omit()

dm_res <- forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)

round(dm_res$statistic, 3)
format.pval(dm_res$p.value, digits = 3)
```

Conclusion -

Because the p-value is well below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of equal forecast accuracy and conclude that the difference in predictive accuracy between the two models is statistically significant.

## Rolling-Window Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| label: cv-rolling
gas_rolling_fc <- can_gas |>  
  select(Month, Volume) |>  
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>  
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),        
    tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())
  ) |>  
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_rolling_fc |>  
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |> 
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Rolling-Window Forecast Accuracy (240-Month Window)")
```

Window Comparison -

The accuracy of the TSLM model improves more noticeably under a rolling window than SNAVIE. Because the linear trend model assumes a static slope, restricting the training sample to a rolling 240-month window prevents long-past historical trends from distorting local slope estimation, enabling the model to adapt dynamically to structural changes.

## 5. Reflection

The residual diagnostics from the linear trend and seasonal dummy model in Part 4.4c clearly indicated that the error terms were not white noise, showing strong autocorrelation and uncaptured cyclical momentum. While the fixed linear trend and static monthly dummies account for baseline growth and predictable calendar shifts, they fail to model dynamic serial dependence where an above-average month is typically followed by another above-average month. To capture this remaining structure, a superior model would likely incorporate autoregressive processes or dynamic trend specifications that allow the trend and seasonal patterns to evolve adaptively over time rather than remaining rigid.
